title: Laudato Si' (2015)
hook: Francis writes on care for our common home

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict's Caritas in Veritate, charity in truth. Your line was the logic of gift. Did you give a little more than the deal required? Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

"Laudato si', mi' Signore." Praised be you, my Lord. That's a line from a song Francis of Assisi wrote, in his own Italian dialect, praising God through Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Wind, Sister Water, and, as he puts it, our sister, Mother Earth. Centuries later, a pope who took Francis's name borrowed that line for the title of a letter. Not about prayer, exactly. About rivers, air, soil, the poor, and the way they're tied together. Pope Francis addressed it not only to Catholics but to everyone living on the planet, and he gave it a subtitle: on care for our common home. Today's word is the idea at the center of it.
screen: `PRAISED BE YOU, MY LORD.` → `A SAINT'S SONG, A POPE'S LETTER.` → `OUR COMMON HOME.`

segments.voice: Francis calls the idea integral ecology. Integral means whole, nothing left out. First, the whole includes us. Ecology often sounds like it's about nature over there: forests, whales, glaciers. Francis says we are part of nature, included in it, not looking at it from outside. We're inside creation, and what we do to it we're doing to ourselves and to each other. Second, the crises are one crisis. Francis argues there aren't two separate problems, one environmental and one social. There's a single, complex crisis that is both. Polluted water and poverty, he says, often land on the same people. So caring for the earth and caring for the poor can't be split into separate departments. Third, the root is in the heart. He doesn't stop at policy. He talks about habits: buying without thinking, using things up, rushing. He calls for an ecological conversion, a change of heart that shows up in small daily acts, like turning off unneeded lights, using less plastic, cooking only what will be eaten. Fourth, it starts in praise. Before it's a duty, it's wonder. The book of Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims, says: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." Very good, before anyone had used them for anything. Francis returns again and again to a phrase that sums all this up, and it's today's line: everything is connected. A choice at a grocery store, a factory far away, a family's water, a bird's nest, God's delight. One web.
screen: `WE ARE INSIDE CREATION, NOT SPECTATORS.` · `ONE CRISIS, BOTH SOCIAL AND NATURAL.` · `CONVERSION SHOWS IN SMALL HABITS.` · `IT STARTS IN PRAISE.` · then, large: `AND THEY WERE VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step outside and give thanks. If you can, go to a door or a window, or out onto a step. If you can't, close your eyes and remember the last time you stood outdoors. Notice one living thing: a tree, a weed in a crack, a bird, the sky itself. Look at it long enough to see something you missed. Then follow one thread: the water it needs, the air you share with it. If you pray, you can say Francis of Assisi's line, praised be you, my Lord. If you don't, simply let yourself be glad it's there. The bell holds the time.
Integral ecology. The whole picture: the earth, the poor, our habits and our praise, held together as one. Today's word.
Your line: everything is connected. Today, pick one thing you throw out, and follow it in your mind one step past the trash can. Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes and schools read Laudato Si' in study groups, some keep a Season of Creation in early autumn, and some form care-for-creation teams that work on energy, waste and local gardens.

original.note: Not Latin: the Umbrian Italian of Francis of Assisi's song, praised be you, my Lord.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pope's letter about recycling.
what it means: a letter on care for our common home, where the earth, the poor, our habits and our praise are one connected whole.
what a scholar hears: a title borrowed from Francis of Assisi's Canticle of the Creatures, and a refusal to split ecology from justice.

notes: Paraphrases of Laudato Si' to confirm: addressed to every person living on this planet; humans are not spectators of creation; 'one complex crisis which is both social and environmental' (ch. 4); ecological conversion (ch. 6) with small daily acts as examples; the recurring phrase 'everything is connected'.
'Polluted water and poverty often land on the same people' is a paraphrase of Laudato Si's discussion of water and the poor; confirm wording is fair.
Canticle spelling: 'Laudato si', mi' Signore' as in the encyclical's opening; confirm pronunciation guide.
howItsDone mentions the Season of Creation and parish care-for-creation teams; confirm.

Editor pass: 'not spectators' replaced with a closer paraphrase of Laudato Si' (part of nature, included in it); daily-act examples aligned with the encyclical's own list (lights, plastic, cooking only what will be eaten) instead of 'sharing a meal'.
